Listen here. LIVE Updated 34 mins ago Rate decision live: Interest rates held steady in split vote, Warsh says politics played 'no role' ahead of midterm elections
 Yahoo Finance Updated Wed, October 28, 2026 at 2:52 PM CST 1 min read Federal Reserve officials voted 10-2 to keep interest rates unchanged, as elevated inflation continues to pose a problem for central bankers. Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring a quarter-point rate hike. 
 The Fed's benchmark rates remained in the 3.75% to 4% range , as widely expected. A rate hike in December, however, appears far more likely, according to the Fed's dot plot and fed funds futures. 
 Here are the key takeaways from the Fed's statement and Fed Chairman Warsh's press conference: 
 Fed upgrades economy from "solid" to "strong": The FOMC updated the language in its statement, adding that "the accumulation of more information will help" it decide the right policy stance. This suggests the Fed is not in a hurry to ease inflation. 
 But "inflation remains elevated": Warsh reiterated the Fed's commitment to bringing inflation down to the 2% target. Although recent inflation data came in hotter than expected , the Fed has positioned itself to continue assessing data. 
 Warsh announces changes to the Fed's schedule : In 2027, one of the eight Fed meetings will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy with neither a vote on the Fed's funds rate nor a policy statement. In 2028, policymakers will hold two meetings dedicated to strategy and six for setting policy. 
 Warsh refutes the idea that the decision was politically inflected: Warsh stated that "politics played no role in the decision" — something that generated some discussion with the US midterm elections next week. 
 LIVE 34 updates 37 mins ago Jennifer Schonberger Warsh quashes Bill Ackman's theory that Fed rate hikes won't impact demand for AI
 Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said he doesn't agree that Fed rate hikes will have no impact on artificial intelligence, given the strong demand for AI and the high returns investors expect. 
 "I was skeptical of that view," Warsh said during a press conference. "Interest rates get in the cracks. Interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything." 
 Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman, in a post last month on X , expressed skepticism that higher rates would reduce demand and investment in AI. 
 "What if higher rates don't reduce demand and investment because the demand for intelligence and energy is unaffected by higher rates because winning the race for super intelligence has a near infinite ROI and the demand for compute will remain incalculable," Ackman wrote. "What if the old models don't apply to the current paradigm?" 
 Warsh pointed to how credit spreads for certain assets have widened since the Fed raised rates in September, and financial conditions have tightened as investors have differentiated between tech firms and other companies to invest. 
 "With respect to the new technology and this investment surge, do interest rates matter? I believe they do," said Warsh. "And I don't believe that they're somehow divorced from the rest of the economy." 
 45 mins ago Ben Werschkul 'I didn't hear an utterance about politics': Warsh bats away midterm talk following rate decision
 Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh pushed back Wednesday on any suggestion that next week's midterm elections had a role in the Fed's decision to keep interest rates steady . He also dodged multiple questions on political topics and pressure coming his way from the Oval Office. 
 But it wasn't for a lack of trying from the assembled reporters. 
 "I appreciate the question, but I'm not going to be responding to quotes from public officials," Warsh said during a press conference when presented with criticisms from President Trump that interest rates should be lower and that his colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee were "political." 
 When the subject turned to the midterm elections, Warsh was similarly curt. 
 "Politics played no role in the decision," the chair said, adding, "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics." 
 Read more. 
 Today at 7:51 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell The Fed just removed a 2027 rate decision — making the remaining 7 even more important
 Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban writes: 
 The Warsh Fed's taciturn nature has already raised the stakes for each FOMC meeting. With fewer hints or forward guidance about what the Fed is thinking and planning comes more suspense. 
 And next year, those stakes will be even higher as the Fed removes a rate decision from its calendar, making each meeting even more important and potentially adding another layer of uncertainty and volatility to markets . 
 At the October policy meeting on Wednesday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced this major change to the Fed's calendar and added that 2028 might feature only six rate decisions. The meetings themselves will remain on the calendar, but instead of the Fed debating rates, broader monetary policy topics will be on the agenda. 
 Warsh said the reasoning behind the schedule change is to "reserve the time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons." 
 We've all been wondering how the newly installed chair would reshape the Fed. Already, he's been doing that by changing the nature of the Fed's public communication. 
 Read more. 
 Today at 7:06 PM UTC Jared Blikre Stocks whipsaw as long-term yields climb after the Fed
 Wall Street can't make up its mind about the Fed. 
 Stocks dipped after the 2 p.m. statement, rallied as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke, then gave much of that back. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) is holding a small gain, and chip stocks are doing most of the lifting. 
 The typical stock isn't doing as well. The equal-weighted S&P 500, which gives every company the same weight, is in the red. So are small caps. 
 The bond market is clearer about what it thinks. The 30-year Treasury yield is near its high of the day, and the 10-year yield is back above 5%. Higher long-term rates make borrowing more expensive for companies and homebuyers. 
 The dollar moved the other way and slipped against the euro during the press conference. 
 That leaves the streak. The S&P 500 came into Wednesday down on six straight Fed days, the second-longest run since 1994, which we pointed out at 2:43 p.m. ET. A higher close would end it, and a lower one would tie the 2018 record of seven. 
 Today at 7:01 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Warsh says politics played 'no role' in decision to hold rates steady
 Chairman Warsh said a couple of words on the Fed's independence amid some discussion that the US midterm elections — just six days away — and the perception that the Fed could influence them could sway the Fed's decision. 
 "Politics played no role in the decision," Warsh stated. "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics." 
 "But I will say," Warsh added, "it's an information-rich interval in the coming period, having nothing to do with politics." 
 Today at 6:53 PM UTC Jared Blikre Bond traders still see more Fed hikes ahead
 The Fed won't be sitting on its hands for long, says the market. 
 Traders see about an 85% chance that the Fed raises its benchmark rate by a quarter point at its next meeting on Dec. 9, according to Bloomberg data. The data comes from futures contracts that let traders bet on where the Fed sets rates. Those odds are about where they stood Tuesday, before the decision. 
 Further out, traders expect the Fed's rate to climb from about 3.9% now to nearly 4.7% by September 2027. That's about three more quarter-point hikes, slightly more than they expected Tuesday. 
 The Dec. 9 meeting is next. A hike would match what traders already expect. Another hold would mean they've gotten ahead of the Fed. 
 Today at 6:49 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Warsh: 'Monetary medicine starting to work some'
 Chairman Warsh noted that while the Fed waits to assess more inflation data, some policymakers view the central bank's moves so far as beginning to take effect. 
 "If you were listening next to me in that room the last couple of days, the overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgment, is that what we've done in this monetary medicine starting to work some, but there's no firm conclusions," Warsh said. 
 "If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today," he added. "What we decided to do was to call these questions, take stock of where we are, evaluate what we're seeing out the window, ask ourselves whether the period right in front of us is likely to provide more clarity on the appropriate protocol." 
 Today at 6:47 PM UTC Ines Ferré Warsh announces changes to FOMC meetings schedule starting next fall 
 Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced a change to the FOMC meeting starting next fall. 
 Warsh said eight meetings per year is the right number for the Federal Open Market Committee. But in 2027, one meeting will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy with neither a vote on the Fed's funds rate nor a policy statement. 
 The rest will be regular policy meetings. Warsh also expects that in 2028, policymakers will hold two meetings dedicated to strategy and six for setting policy. 
 "Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals," said Warsh. 
 "But it's equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons," he added. 
 Today at 6:43 PM UTC Jared Blikre Stocks have lost on six straight Fed days
 Stocks have a Fed-day problem. 
 The S&P 500 (^GSPC) came into Wednesday down on six straight Fed days, according to Bespoke Investment Group . That's the second-longest streak since 1994, when the Fed began announcing its decisions on meeting day. The record is seven, and it peaked with Jerome Powell's December 2018 rate hike, in the middle of that quarter's sell-off. 
 The current streak covers two chairs. It started late in Powell's term, and Kevin Warsh's first three meetings extended it. The S&P 500 averaged a decline of more than 1% on those three days, per Bespoke , by far the worst start for any modern chair. 
 Most of the damage came after the 2 p.m. statement. In Bespoke's composite of each chair's first three meetings, stocks under Warsh drifted sideways all morning, then fell about 1% into the close. Bernanke's and Yellen's early meetings both finished higher. 
 A lower close Wednesday would tie the 2018 record. With two officials dissenting in favor of a hike, Warsh's press conference has a lot to explain. 
 Today at 6:39 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Warsh 'unwilling' to call financial conditions 'tight'
 Chairman Warsh said that despite September's rate hike, he still believes financial conditions aren't yet tight: 
 "Market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations, and while overall financial conditions are tighter, I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight," Warsh said. 
 Today at 6:36 PM UTC Molly Moorhead Realtor.com economist: Mortgage rates will remain volatile
 The Fed's decision to hold interest rates steady will do little to unlock the stagnant housing market. 
 Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale noted in a statement Wednesday that bond yields have been rising, bringing mortgage rates higher to an average of around 7.4% on a 30-year loan. 
 "Mortgage rates have not dropped back to their mid-September level, and the housing market is feeling the effects," Hale said. 
 She pointed to September pending home sales, which hit the lowest level since 2001 . 
 "Those hoping to make a home purchase in the months ahead should plan for further mortgage rate volatility," Hale said. 
 Today at 6:34 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Warsh calls out 'strong' economic activity, reiterates commitment to 'deliver price stability'
 Chairman Warsh's assessment of the economy is that it remains resilient; however, he reiterated the Fed's commitment to bringing inflation down: 
 "Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace, while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments. Domestic spending has been resilient, productivity growth is strong, and capital investment robust," Warsh said in his opening remarks. 
 "Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little. But inflation remains elevated. The committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2% goal. The committee will deliver price stability." 
 Today at 6:31 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Fed press conference begins...
 Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has taken the podium. You can watch the press conference live here: 
 Today at 6:27 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Treasury yields rise, fixed-income investor warns of imminent communication mistake
 Treasury yields are edging higher ahead of Chairman Warsh's press conference. 
 The 10-year yield ( ^TNX ) rose 5 basis points to 5.04%, and the 30-year yield ( ^TYX ) is up 2 basis points to 5.33%. 
 "I think we're setting ourselves up for a potential communication mistake in the press conference that we're about to have," Christian Hoffmann, Thornburg Investment Management head of fixed income, told Yahoo Finance. "The last one was fairly smooth, but I think the risk is to the downside over the next 45 minutes." 
 Today at 6:21 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Warsh looking to control the narrative amid rate pause: Economist
 Stocks are little changed as there were no real fireworks in the Fed's decision to keep rates steady. 
 But according to EY-Parthenon chief economist Gregory Daco, what Kevin Warsh says next could shape how investors view the Fed's policy stance right now, with some economist expecting a "hawkish hold" tilt. 
 "Controlling the narrative is what is important from Fed Chair Warsh," Daco told Yahoo Finance. "As he speaks for the committee, … he is the one that is guiding markets' interpretation of the Fed's next move." 
 "We know he does not want to communicate," Daco added. "He does not want to spoon-feed markets, as he said in the past. But he has an essential role in communicating how the Fed is thinking about the economic outlook and risks to the outlook. That's very important." 
 Daco says Warsh will need to at least explain how the Fed will adjust policy for upside risks and downside risks in this environment to avoid more market volatility. 
 Today at 6:10 PM UTC Jared Blikre Fed adjusts language on the economy, guidance, and vote
 Here's another way to look at the four places the Fed's statement changed from September (see blog below). 
 The decision: "Raise" became "maintain." The Fed kept its target range at 3.75%-4% instead of adding another quarter point. 
 The economy: Growth was upgraded to a "strong" pace from "solid." 
 The guidance: The Fed dropped "Today's policy action will support" a return to 2% inflation. In its place, "the accumulation of more information will help" it decide the right stance. "Timelier" also became "timely," so the Fed is in less of a hurry to get inflation down. 
 The vote: It went from 12-0 to 10-2. Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissented because they wanted another quarter-point hike. 
 Today at 6:09 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Here are the changes to the FOMC statement
 In the FOMC statement, the rate-setting committee emphasized that the Fed remains committed to a "timely return" to the committee's 2% inflation target. 
 Here are all the changes to the Fed's statement, with additions in bold and deletions struck through: 
 The Committee decided to raise maintain the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system. 
 Economic activity is expanding at a solid strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little. 
 Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action The accumulation of more information will support help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timelier timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability. 
 Today at 6:02 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Fed holds interest rates steady in a range of 3.75% to 4%
 The Federal Reserve kept interest rates unchanged on Wednesday in the 3.75% to 4% range, as economists expected. 
 The vote was split 10-2. Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring a quarter-point rate hike. 
 While the decision offered little surprise to Fed watchers, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's press conference at 2:30 p.m. ET will be closely watched for clues on the Fed's thinking on inflation and the December FOMC meeting. 
 Today at 5:44 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Stocks muted ahead of Fed decision
 Markets are having a muted day so far, with less than half an hour to go until the Fed decision. 
 The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) is up 0.2%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) is leading the indexes, up 0.3%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) has been trading roughly flat. 
 The US dollar index ( DX-Y.NYB ) is also little changed at 102. The 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ) edged higher by 3 basis points to 5.02%. 
 Our stock market live blog will follow the market's reaction to the FOMC statement. 
 Today at 4:30 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Will another rate hike happen by the end of the year?
 Yahoo Finance's Ivana Pino writes: 
 At the beginning of 2026, the biggest question surrounding the Federal Reserve and interest rates was whether the Fed would cut its target rate at some point this year. However, it's become increasingly clear that a rate cut won't happen any time soon. In fact, the Fed raised its target rate for the first time in over three years in September, and it's possible that another rate hike will happen before the year is over. 
 … For example, the Fed's latest dot plot indicated that a second rate hike is expected in 2026. However, CME's FedWatch tool predicts less than a 10% chance of a rate hike following the conclusion of this week's Fed meeting . 
 "Interest rate markets currently expect one or two rate increases," said Gary Pzegeo, CFA and chief investment officer at CIBC Private Wealth, a fee-based financial advisor firm headquartered in Chicago. "Energy prices cooled in June, but the escalation of hostilities in the Middle East have led to an increase in global crude oil prices and retail gasoline prices at home." 
 Pzegeo added, "it is difficult to predict how geopolitical events will play out, but the current trend would suggest the Fed will follow through with a rate hike to cool demand and offset the reduction in energy supply." He noted that if the Fed does raise rates, consumers should expect the cost of borrowing money to increase.
